projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Leonard Carey was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: In 1949 -- '41 when I was list -- living in Akron, Ohio, and it was on a Sunday morning, December 7th that we received that news. May I tell you about that morning?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes, please.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, many of us being at age 17 felt so compelled about defending our Country after being invaded in Pearl Harbor that we decided that we, of our own volition, would enlist, and that's primarily what I was going to tell you, that many, many veterans undoubtedly told you that, Tom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you enlisted how soon after December 7th?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I would say -- let's see -- I would say I enlisted June which would be -- which would be the following June and -- and I already -- I was attending college being under age I was there and then enlisted and went immediately into the Navy. I went into their V-6 program at Bowling Green State University for officer training and during the course of my training it was closed after Columbia University. So, then I retrained myself, or they retrained me as a motor machinist's mate and went overseas to British Mandate Island after a short period in New Guinea, but this was Admiralty Islands in the South Pacific, and we were in a repair base for the United States Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, at that age did you have to get parental permission to enlist?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I did. My parents gave me permission because they saw the gravity of it and certainly the seriousness that I had in trying to defend our Country. Now, when I received retraining in -- as a motor machinist's mate, they shipped me then to -- took us three days by train to get there to the west coast and put us on what -- it was the Mannis Island, the Mannis Transportation Ship Company, and they transported down the Navy personnel but also troop personnel that they were dropping off at all the islands. Took us about twice as long to get to our destination because we were tacking, varying our course to avoid submarine attack. So, it took us a whole month, 30 days to get there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And this was from the west coast to --

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: From the west coast to New Guinea across the International Dateline and then we finally settled on this group of islands, the Admiralty Islands to start repairing huge battleships and cruisers. I'd like to tell you something about an operation there on the islands that we as Navy veterans feel very proud about. It was a -- it was a unit that had a number of -- if you could envision this -- a number of quonset-type repair shops and when we received parts which were in grease from Rosie the riveters back home. They removed all the grease. They brought the parts into machine shops and machined them to specifications, and they also brought them into what they called a clean room which would give last minute adjustments to the Bosch injectors for diesel engines. So, that was the scope of our operation. It was very, very complete. And what was most inspiring for us is to look out on the bay and see three -- not one but three dry docks, each dry dock holding seven sections to be put together, and when submerged under the keel of a disabled battleship, these battleships were literally lifted up high and dry out of the water and huge holes were displayed at that time and our welders who took -- who had a supply of battleship welding plates to put on went in there and repaired everything like it was just brand new. And -- and to go home after the war each of these seven sections in each dry dock were sailed back home, and they were pulled one section at a time over to the United States again. Most of the supplies we left for economic reasons were left on the islands. When we were stationed there and worked in repair bases, we encountered many air raids from the Japanese and we had literally no guns to defend ourselves. We were prey to them, and we managed to survive.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they think it was a safe area that you didn't need anti-aircraft?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: They felt that since we were removed from the battling islands that they could not provide the provisions to defend us; and when it comes to my experience personally as a 19-year-old but by the time -- I was 19 by the time I arrived there, we were stationed inspirationally with a group of older men, they were 34 years of age on the average, and those were the men who came out of industry, and they were the ones who did most of the machining of the parts and the welding and everything, and we "kids" as they called us did the office work and things like that to keep the operation going and the ordering and whatnot. So, we were inspired to be with a little older group of men; but we felt that we were a tremendous help to them. Would you like to ask me any questions, Tom?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you get overseas?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I arrived overseas I would say in 1944, and I stayed there a year and a half; and then when we came back, I was discharged from the South Pacific to home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you mentioned the trip, did you have any actual sub scares?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: No. We had two harrowing experiences which are pretty common to sailors. We had not one but three tidal waves that we encountered. The waves were just one wave -- each encounter. They would rise out of the sea anywhere from 20 to 60 feet, one wave, and our ship was battered about as you've encountered many times the -- half the trip had the screw of the ship coming out of the water and then when it settled back you heard a tremendous booming of the screw settling back into the water. We had about five or six major storms and it was quite an encounter because being on the water 30 days you did encounter all kinds of weather.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you part of a convoy?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: No, we were by ourselves.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to eat at all during that with the rocky seas?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, it was quite a big operation onboard that ship. It was a complete -- a little island in itself. They had their own cooking staff. They put us up -- I'm glad you ask that question. They put us up -- both in the hold and on open decks and that was my -- my billet. It was on top deck and each -- each Quonset hut or each bunk was built eight high on an open -- open deck that way and that's the way we lived for those 30 days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the name of that ship?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: It was called the Mannis Island or the Mannis ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit. Do you have any memorable experiences from your training before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: We had most of our memorable experiences onboard that ship going over. And I'll tell you a little bit about the lifestyle on the island in a little -- in a few minutes, but -- but going over we were served by a Navy crew and we had some humorous experiences. We didn't live very -- very well onboard ship. It was a spartan experience and one of the many, many fellow sailors that I sailed with was tremendously humorous. He name was Butte Hash (ph) from Detroit, Michigan, and he would come up from the chow hall and say "Boy that -- that -- those noodles on rice was -- and bacon was really delicious." Well, one of my best buddies took him and held him over the edge of the ship and said, "If you say anything about this food once more, I'm going to drop you."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any really close buddies when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Many of them. I'm glad you brought that up. I was a year older than my Navy buddies -- and they came immediately from high school into the service. As I said, I was already attending college for a year and -- and they were all from the New England states, primarily Massachusetts and New Hampshire, and after about 45 years time I looked up Hugh Cassidy from Concord, Massachusetts, and called up through information the Cassidy residence and this gentleman said "Why, yes, this is the Cassidy residence; but you want to speak to my son. I'm in a nursing home." So, we did reunite the three of us and Hugh Cassidy and John Carol his buddy, my buddy, we were very close throughout all our experience overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do for entertainment, for instance, when you had a chance to take a break?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I'm glad you mentioned that. We were not allowed to leave our station. It was a very important aspect of the operation of the South Pacific and so usually we went to -- we attended a movie once every three weeks and it was -- everything was built like a Quonset hut, whether it was the cafeteria or whether it was an arena-type entertainment center, and we would sit in a driving rain just to see a movie.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any of the movies that they showed?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Mainly they were movies that were old variety from James Stewart, people like that. Now, our island was not only a repair island, but it was sort of a weigh station for many, many transient troops. Most of our troops that we saw set foot on our island for a day of rest. Most of the troops were from Australia and they were very respectful to us and we were considerate of them, because we knew that they would be pushing on to pretty dangerous areas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of any particularly frightening air raids?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, we had -- usually an air raid warning happened on the average about once a week. I don't know whether they actually came close to our islands or not, but we had to leave our Quonset hut and then dove into the ditch whenever they -- whenever they bombed us and that's another humorous experience. One of the retiring Navy chiefs couldn't wait to get home and he was due in the middle of the war to be discharged because of nerves and whatnot -- we said that they're coming and they're ready to bomb us and he being intoxicated dove for the gutter again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't get any U.S.O. shows or anything like that, did you?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: No, we did not. We lived a very spartan life, and on Sundays, occasionally, we would have a Navy chaplain give service. We worked and lived around the clock. We were a 24-hour island that repaired ships night and day. It was your duty and your expectation to work on the islands each of these three shifts. The morning shift, the grave shift -- no, the swing shift was the second one and then the grave shift. And frequently we had breakfast served to us at midnight before we went to work in the grave shift. [Interview interrupted.]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's see, where were we?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, we were at the point where you asked about the operation 24 hours a day there on the islands at the repair base. And when it came to maintaining the island that is with varying duties I worked in office for the officers and put out bulletins for the day, but if there was -- they called it a typhoon, but it amounted to a hurricane. That was our -- that's the United States terminology. Whenever that came in, just to give you an idea of the type of maintenance of the island, we all had duties to take landing craft, lighter weight ships -- not the dry docks -- in towards the coast and we were responsible in landing craft, for example, to tow them out of the harm of a rough sea around the islands. So, that's just the very basic way of saying that whether we were assigned cooking duties or whether it was administrative duties, we did maintain the island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not to get too technical, but how did they actually raise the dry dock of the battleship?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Did you ask about the weight of the dry dock?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, yeah, for instance you were talking about raising the battleships out of the --

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Oh, that was quite an operation. The dry dock itself was bigger than three football fields, the area, and these were air, independent ballasts, each of the seven ballasts would be filled with water and they would be submerged, I would say, around 70, 80, maybe 90 feet under water. The top of the dry dock would just barely show at the -- at the surface of the water. And then we would have tugboats pushing the dry dock under the battleship itself or the cruiser or whatever had to be repaired. And once it was under there and firmly lashed to the side of our dry dock, they began to pump the water out of the dry dock and everything would rise to the surface.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, basically the same way a submarine would surface?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Just like a submarine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: And you could imagine the technology -- the technical training of all of this -- these Navy personnel not only from the standpoint of the submerged dry dock -- that operation, but also the welders as I said and the repairmen on the ship -- at each ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particularly famous ships that might have passed through the repair gates?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: We had the New York --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: -- battleship. And that one stands out particularly in my mind, but we would repair say cruisers which were smaller, five or six at a time. So, it was quite a big operation. I was inspired to be there. I felt as though I was really an integral part of helping.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, that was your station the whole time you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes. When the time came for discharging -- these older gentlemen who worked with us were discharged first because they were older and they had a -- and then you were given points for discharging if you were married and had children and whatnot. So, they left first and -- and when we were transferred at this island complex, a number of islands, when we were transferred from one base to another, why we always took our provisions with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memories of mail call, getting packages from home that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, we received packages from home almost on a weekly basis; and I'm glad you brought that point up. There were many, many incidents at home that were not brought to our attention from our family as our families, as far as their sacrifices were concerned, but they did go out of their way to take any ration provision they had to spare and mail me packages, and usually I -- usually always I shared them with all of my buddies and they did likewise with me, but it was very close-knit group of people. And you asked if we were close, yes, we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would they send?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, they would send mostly things that could be shipped and not lost in transit; foodwise, usually canned goods and my mother sent us many, many fruit cakes which I don't appreciate today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would hold up in the trip overseas. Were you able to write much back to them?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I'm glad you mentioned that. I had a number of women friends that I wrote to. They were the only ones in the island -- back home and they were usually family of my Navy buddies and I would write like a 10- or 12-page letter to Eleanor Elbracht (ph). Her mother lived in the Collinwood (ph) area and they were raised there and she would always -- she would never talk about the sacrifices she made here in the United States but I did write quite often and that was our main avenue of relief.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could you tell them where you were specifically?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: On the islands themselves?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: The -- the islands themselves were not named. They were numbered.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: And it was -- we were not stationed inland. It was all on the coast of each island.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, one of the Admiralty Islands?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes, one of the Admiralty Islands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you were -- let's see, you were probably there until the end of the war I assume?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes, I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of the day that F.D.R. died?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: This happened in April.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: And it was a very sad series of weeks put together about him because we had the utmost of admiration for the executive leader of our Country and to experience him passing away it was very, very traumatic to us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the reaction of most of the men there?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes, it was. Yes, it was. (Inaudible.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the thoughts about Mr. Truman? Did they know anything about it?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: They didn't know anything about Harry Truman but later, years later, we found out how profound he was in the decisions he made immediately upon the president's demise and also in his succession of presidency, but he was a very brilliant man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the feeling at that time that an invasion of Japan was imminent?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes. We felt that we lock, stock and barrel would have to get closer, and we would have to leave the Admiralty Islands and go and invade Japan. We were ready to leave our function as a repair base and actually engage in battle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you feel about that?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Gave it no thought at all. We felt it was our duty.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, then no memories of the day you heard the bombs had been dropped, the first bomb had been dropped?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes. When we received word about the bombing of Nagasaki, we did not -- we had remorse for the citizens of Japan. We were not calloused at all. I would like to believe that World War II veterans were not cold-hearted people but sort of compassionate people. I think that's -- you could sum up who we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But the reaction was it's a necessary evil?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: There were differences of opinion about that. Personally since I've a deep religious background I felt that it was unnecessary. But what happened after the bombing I suppose is what precipitated the end of the war, I'm just guessing that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, how did you celebrate on J.V. day?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, when the war was over, there was a definite relaxed attitude; but we still went about our business of engaging in the maintenance of the island and the operation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No big parties or wild celebrations?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: No, we didn't celebrate that way. I think it really matured us greatly and I'll tell you about what happened to me after the war, getting back to show you the maturity in which work can inflict upon Veterans. The Veterans Administration permitted any of us who wanted to go to college under the Veterans Administration, the G.I. Bill, to attend and when I returned back to my college, which was Ken State University, we were known as six-year college students, three in the service and three in the university and they -- the 18-year-old children who came out of high school to attend college hated us because of the seriousness of which we carried on in our studies, and we did not go to college in four years. We went summers and the regular school year. So, that shows you about the seriousness of our commitment to return to civilian life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. When did you finally get home?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, I arrived home around April of 1946 and coming down Main Street you've heard many, many stories about celebrations. Well, mine was a quiet, peaceful, reflective return home down Main Street in Akron and I saw within a three-year period the changes that took place mostly of a very simplistic nature instead of something elaborate, it was just the opposite, but yet I was glad to be home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after military life?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: I would say most of us had trouble adjusting because we felt that -- that -- we did not have remorse for losing three or four years of our lives, but we did feel that the young people around us were not as appreciative as they could have been when it comes to the real values of freedom. Ask me that when I was just 21 and returning I wouldn't be able to express it in that light, but after many years, I've thought about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, what I thought was most -- upper most in my mind was the fact that we were a cohesive unit and that we did contribute a major part of keeping our troops as well prepared as they were. That was the major feeling that we had and still have to this day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you loose anybody to any accidents or air raids (inaudible)?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: We lost them in air raids. We had military memorials then overseas. So, yes, that was primarily uppermost in our minds when -- when those tragic things happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, comes the free form portion of the interview. Whatever else that I haven't covered that I haven't asked you about, can you think of anything else?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, the primary thing I want to bring to your attention, Tom, as I tried to say there at the Geauga County Fair is that the people back home were so supportive -- and I'm not just talking about my parents -- but they were very, very willing to make sacrifices of their own, sacrifices that we had no idea was going on at the time. So, speaking freely and impromptu, I think we were all in this thing together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that is what seems to make this experience unique?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Yes, it does. Yes, it does. I don't know of another confrontation in war with -- at any other period that had this cohesiveness that we have had, both civilians and military people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: Well, that's fine, Tom, and thank you for coming. I just wanted to let you know about the operation of a repair base overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Inaudible.)

sp.speaker: Leonard Carey
sp.p: And thank you for coming. (Interview concluded.)
